hops.afterHeading: The idea: three steps, and a drug changes mainly one
hops.title: The Calabar bean in a surgeon's own eye
hops.text: On January 17, 1863, the Edinburgh eye surgeon Douglas Argyll Robertson put a drop of extract from the Calabar bean, a West African poison, into his own left eye. Twenty minutes later that pupil was half the width of his right. The bean's alkaloid, physostigmine, inhibits acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine lingers at the iris and keeps the pupil small. Atropine acts at a different step: it sits in the muscarinic receptor without activating it. Argyll Robertson showed that atropine opposes the bean, and physostigmine went on to become the first effective glaucoma medication.

hops.title: Ivermectin, golf-course soil and glutamate as a brake
hops.text: In your brain, glutamate mostly excites. In roundworms, glutamate also opens chloride channels that dampen neuron excitability, so at those channels the same molecule works as a brake. In the 1970s the microbiologist Satoshi Ōmura isolated a bacterium, Streptomyces avermitilis, from soil near a golf course in Ito, Japan. Its avermectin, modified into ivermectin, binds the worm channels in their membrane-spanning region and holds them open. Chloride flows in and the worms' nerve and muscle cells go quiet. The young worms behind river blindness are disabled, and the evidence suggests the patient's immune system then clears them. That scoop of golf-course soil earned a share of the 2015 Nobel Prize.

sources.citation: The Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet. The 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine — Advanced Information. 2015.

hops.afterHeading: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K
hops.title: Coffee does not give your brain energy
hops.text: Coffee feels like fuel, but caffeine supplies no energy at all. It is an adenosine receptor antagonist: it sits in brain receptors for adenosine, a chemical cue for sleepiness, without activating them. In 2012, researchers used PET scans in 15 volunteers to estimate how many brain A1 adenosine receptors caffeine fills. Their fitted curve put half occupancy at about 67 micromolar caffeine in plasma, and they concluded that steady coffee drinking through a day might fill up to half of these receptors. In the lesson's competitive model, caffeine sitting at its KB would make adenosine need twice its usual concentration for the same receptor response.

sources.citation: Elmenhorst D, Meyer PT, Matusch A, Winz OH, Bauer A. Caffeine occupancy of human cerebral A1 adenosine receptors: in vivo quantification with 18F-CPFPX and PET. J Nucl Med. 2012;53(11):1723-1729.
